title: AI as Math Tutor: Helpful Tool or Harmful Crutch?
summary:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly finding its way into classrooms, but is it a good math tutor? A new survey of 1,300 high school students from the U.S., England, and Wales—all participants in an international math contest—offers a nuanced answer: AI can be a powerful learning aid, but only when used strategically.

The survey, conducted by the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics, found that about half of the students believed AI could be an effective tutor if used in specific ways, such as explaining concepts in multiple ways, checking homework, and answering "why" questions to deepen understanding. More than 60 percent of the 200-plus teachers surveyed agreed that AI tutoring could be beneficial.

However, the key is how students use it. Robbie Torney of Common Sense Media, who was not involved in the survey, emphasizes that learning requires "friction"—the productive struggle of grappling with difficult problems. "AI was designed to reduce friction," he notes, but that can undermine learning. Tiago C.P., a Colorado high school senior, puts it simply: "I won't use AI before I've fully attempted a problem."

The survey found that 63 percent of students always try a problem on their own first. When stuck, they prefer asking teachers (58 percent) or classmates (50 percent) before turning to AI (39 percent). This suggests AI should be a last resort, not a first stop.

Teachers' biggest concern, cited by nearly three-quarters of respondents, is that AI can quickly become a crutch. Amanda Brown, a math teacher at Broomfield High School, observes that students with perfect homework scores often fail tests because they relied on AI. "You're gonna have to take the test without AI," she says. "And that's when it comes out: Do you know the material or not?"

The consensus among experts and students is moderation. Amelie M., another Colorado senior, recommends asking AI very specific questions, such as "What are different ways I could solve this?" and adding "Don't give me the answer" to prompts. That way, AI becomes a tool for understanding, not a shortcut to completion.
why_it_matters: As AI becomes a normal study tool, students will need self-regulation and verification habits to avoid widening the gap between homework performance and real understanding. How schools address this could shape learning for a generation.

background_read: AI chatbots such as ChatGPT became widely available to students in late 2022, and schools are still debating whether they support or undermine learning.

The survey comes from the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (a professional organization for applied mathematicians), and it focused on high school students who already participate in an international math contest, so these are motivated learners.

Common Sense Media (a nonprofit that reviews media and technology for families) argues that productive struggle—often called 'friction'—is essential for forming long-term understanding; AI tools tend to remove that friction.
Large language models generate answers by predicting likely words, so they can produce confident-sounding but wrong solutions, especially in multi-step math problems.
Teachers often describe a 'homework-test gap': students who rely on AI at home may score well on assignments but fail exams that require independent recall.

perspectives.description: Students who use AI carefully can get multiple explanations, check their work, and explore why a method works. For motivated learners, AI can act like a patient personal tutor that is available anytime.
Teachers worry that AI removes the productive struggle needed to build deep understanding. Students may earn high homework scores but fail tests, revealing that the learning never really happened.

The survey highlights a broader tension in education technology: tools that reduce friction can make work easier but may weaken the long-term memory and problem-solving skills built through effort. The issue may be less about AI itself and more about how and when it is used.

Schools may need to teach prompt literacy and create policies that require students to try problems independently first. AI could be used to generate similar practice problems or ask guided questions instead of giving answers directly.
